title: Conditions and Decisions
description: Direct program flow using if, else if, and else statements; compose compound boolean conditions using logical operators (&&, ||, !); eliminate accidental assignment and boundary bugs.

objectives.statement: Construct conditional branches using if, else if, and else to execute code based on boolean expressions.
Compose multi-clause boolean expressions using logical AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!).
Diagnose and fix conditional bugs such as accidental assignment in conditions (= vs ===) and improper branch ordering.

content.title: Directing Execution Flow with Decisions
content.hook: Without conditions, programs can only run in a straight line from top to bottom. Conditions give code the power to make decisions.
content.context: Real-world web applications dynamically respond to user state: is the user logged in? Has the form been filled correctly? Is their cart total eligible for free shipping? Using if, else if, and else constructs, we route execution down the exact branch intended.
goals: Master conditional branching with `if`, `else if`, and `else`.
Compose robust multi-clause logic using `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), and `!` (NOT).
Identify and fix the classic accidental assignment bug (`if (x = y)`).
Understand how condition ordering impacts branch selection.

content.title: The Decision Tree: if / else if / else Execution Flow
content.description: Flowchart diagram showing an expression entering condition 1: if true -> runs Branch 1 and exits tree; if false -> evaluates condition 2: if true -> runs Branch 2 and exits tree; if false -> runs default else fallback branch and exits.

content.prompt: What does the following code print to the console?

hints.content: Evaluate each branch in order: 85 >= 90 is false. Then 85 >= 80 is evaluated.
Because 85 >= 80 is true, grade is assigned 'B' and all remaining else if/else branches are bypassed.

feedback.correct: Correct! 85 >= 90 is false, but 85 >= 80 is true. The 'B' branch executes, and JavaScript immediately exits the conditional construct without evaluating subsequent branches.
feedback.incorrect: Trace top to bottom: 85 >= 90 fails, then 85 >= 80 succeeds, setting grade to 'B'. Execution then exits the if/else chain immediately.

options.text: Single equals (=) assigns 'admin' to userRole, which evaluates to a truthy string, granting access to every user regardless of role.
JavaScript throws a SyntaxError and stops execution.
The condition compares 'guest' with 'admin' and returns false.
The if statement treats userRole as undefined.

hints.content: Remember the distinction between = (assignment operator) and === (strict equality comparison).

feedback.correct: Spot on! The single equals operator assigns 'admin' to userRole. The assignment expression evaluates to 'admin', which is a non-empty truthy string, causing the if block to always execute. Comparison requires ===.
feedback.incorrect: Single equals (=) is assignment, not comparison! It overwrites userRole with 'admin', which evaluates to truthy, dangerously executing the access granted branch every time.

content.prompt: Arrange the steps in the exact chronological order that the JavaScript engine follows when processing a multi-branch `if...else if...else` construct:

items.text: Evaluate the condition expression inside the primary if (...) clause.
If truthy, execute the if code block and immediately bypass all remaining branches.
If falsy, sequentially evaluate each else if (...) condition from top to bottom.
If all preceding if and else if conditions were falsy, execute the default else fallback block.

hints.content: JavaScript begins with the initial if condition, executes and exits on the first true branch, evaluates else if branches sequentially if falsy, and falls back to else.

feedback.correct: Perfect sequence! JavaScript evaluates branches sequentially from top to bottom, halting as soon as the first truthy condition is encountered.
feedback.incorrect: Review the flow: 1. Evaluate if condition -> 2. Execute if true and exit -> 3. Evaluate else if conditions if false -> 4. Run else fallback if all conditions fail.

content.title: Build the Lesson Access Router
content.prompt:
Implement the function `getLessonAccess(isEnrolled, isCompleted, prerequisitePassed, userRole)`:
1. If `userRole === 'admin'`, return `'unlocked'` (admins bypass all restrictions).
2. If `!isEnrolled`, return `'not-enrolled'`.
3. If `isCompleted`, return `'completed'`.
4. If `prerequisitePassed`, return `'unlocked'`.
5. If none of the above conditions apply, return `'locked'`.

testCases.description: Admin users receive 'unlocked' regardless of enrollment or prerequisites
Enrolled users with completed lesson receive 'completed'
Enrolled users with prerequisite passed receive 'unlocked'
Enrolled users without prerequisite passed receive 'locked'

hints.content: Start with admin check: if (userRole === 'admin') { return 'unlocked'; }
Chain else if checks: else if (!isEnrolled) { return 'not-enrolled'; } else if (isCompleted) { return 'completed'; } else if (prerequisitePassed) { return 'unlocked'; }
End with the default fallback: else { return 'locked'; }

feedback.correct: Splendid! Your router handles user roles, enrollment flags, and prerequisites in clean, mutually exclusive order.
feedback.incorrect: Review your branch order. Ensure admin is evaluated first, followed by enrollment, completion, prerequisite status, and locked as fallback.

content.prompt: Why does the order of conditions in an if...else if ladder matter so much? What can go wrong if a more general condition is placed above a more specific one?

feedback.correct: Excellent synthesis! Because JavaScript executes only the first matching branch in an if...else if chain, placing a broad condition first will shadow and starve more specific cases below it.
feedback.incorrect: Please articulate your reflection with at least 50 characters, explaining how branch ordering affects mutual exclusivity and prevents condition shadowing.

content.title: Conditions and Decisions Mastery
takeaways: if, else if, and else evaluate boolean conditions sequentially and execute only the first matching branch.
Logical operators (&&, ||, !) allow combining multiple criteria into expressive control expressions.
Accidental assignment inside conditions (if (x = y)) is a dangerous defect prevented by always using strict equality (===).
Condition ordering is critical: specific conditions must precede broader fallback cases.
